questions.prompt: What is the critical difference between `@StateObject` and `@ObservedObject` in SwiftUI? Provide your answer in 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: `@StateObject` creates and owns the lifecycle of an observable object. SwiftUI creates the instance once and preserves it across view redraws. In contrast, `@ObservedObject` does not own the object lifecycle. If you initialize an `@ObservedObject` inline inside a view, it is recreated every time the parent view redraws, losing state.

rubric.criterion: Explains that @StateObject owns the object lifecycle and persists across redraws.
Contrasts with @ObservedObject which does not own the lifecycle.
Explains that inline @ObservedObject causes recreation and state loss on redraw.

questions.prompt: Explain what the `objectWillChange` publisher is and when it fires in Combine. Answer in 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: `objectWillChange` is a Combine publisher required by the `ObservableObject` protocol. When a property marked with `@Published` changes, the publisher automatically sends an event. It fires during the `willSet` phase before the new value is stored. This tells observing SwiftUI views that data is about to change so they can prepare to redraw.

rubric.criterion: Identifies objectWillChange as a publisher from the ObservableObject protocol.
Explains that it fires in willSet before the property value updates.
Explains that it signals observing views to redraw.

questions.prompt: Why can coarse-grained invalidation in `ObservableObject` hurt performance in large view hierarchies? Explain in 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: `ObservableObject` invalidates views at the object level rather than the property level. When any `@Published` property changes, every view observing the object evaluates its body. Even if a view only displays an unchanged property, it still redraws. In large view hierarchies, this creates unnecessary view recalculations and diffing work.

rubric.criterion: States that ObservableObject invalidates at the whole-object level rather than property level.
Explains that views reading unchanged properties still redraw.
Mentions excess body evaluations and diffing overhead in large hierarchies.

questions.prompt: What are the key steps to migrate a legacy `ObservableObject` class to the iOS 17 `@Observable` macro? Answer in 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: First, replace `ObservableObject` protocol conformance with the `@Observable` macro on the class declaration. Second, remove all `@Published` wrappers from stored properties because stored properties are tracked automatically. Finally, update observing views by replacing `@StateObject` with `@State`, and replacing `@ObservedObject` with regular properties or `@Bindable`.

rubric.criterion: Mentions replacing ObservableObject conformance with the @Observable macro.
Mentions removing @Published property wrappers from stored properties.
Mentions replacing @StateObject with @State and @ObservedObject with regular properties or @Bindable.

questions.prompt: Why can using `@EnvironmentObject` lead to runtime crashes, and how do you prevent them? Answer in 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: `@EnvironmentObject` expects an instance of the requested type to be present in the environment. If an ancestor view forgets to call `.environmentObject(model)`, SwiftUI crashes with a fatal runtime exception when the view renders. You can prevent this crash by injecting the model at the root of the navigation hierarchy or by migrating to `@Environment(Model.self)` with optional types.

rubric.criterion: Explains that missing environment objects cause fatal runtime crashes.
Explains root injection or migrating to type-based environment models.
